title: Is this still AI slop?
author: QcyqApps
selftext:
Tidle. I spent over a year developing this game. Then, using AI, I managed to rebuild almost the entire thing in just two weeks, mainly focusing on UX and visuals.

One important thing I want to clarify: the graphics aren't entirely AI-generated from scratch.

I originally created the maps myself using Synty 3D assets. I then fed those maps to AI as visual references, allowing it to recreate and improve the visuals while maintaining the original style and artistic direction.

AI tools have become significantly more capable since I started this project. The results are now much more consistent stylistically and considerably more performant than my previous approach.

So, what do you think? Is this still AI slop, or is this a reasonable way for a solo developer to use AI as a creative and development tool?

**AI disclosure:** [https://tidle.ovh/en/ai/](https://tidle.ovh/en/ai/)

**Play the game:** [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tidle](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tidle)

comments.author: DramaLlamaDad
comments.body:
I own a large MMO that I had put a team on but had largely become stagnant. I came back about 6 months ago and fixed 2800 bugs that had been open for years. The result is they called the game AI slop. Yes, an existing game written by humans, 2.7mln lines of code that was full of bugs and using AI to fix the human bugs made people call it AI slop.

Bottom line is, AI slop is just a pointless made up negative term.  No one ever calls out human slop.  Just ignore 100% of the people who use the phrase AI Slop. If they say that, ask for specific feedback.

People will eventually figure out it is just another tool that enables us to accelerate our work flow and also bring new kinds of content and game play with small teams.

comments.author: alcarcalimo1950
comments.body:
I’m in the process of developing my own game and what is standing out to me see a lot of posts on here is when you think you’re done, you’re not. And really being honest with yourself about the quality. 

There is always room for polish, but when I look at this it doesn’t seem polished at all. I’m heavily using AI in my own development, but every element really gets severely scrutinized by me on an individual basis, and then as a whole. 

Especially for your UI, it’s not even that it looks like AI. It looks like a lot of cash grab mobile games. You really need to define standards for your UI. Things like what’s the proper spacing from borders for icons/text. Really evaluating color and what colors go together. How text looks on background. There is a whole host of other things. I’m not a UI designer by nature, but you have to think at larger companies they have whole teams dedicated to just UI design. It’s an art as much as asset generation. 

As others have said, a lot of the issues with AI assisted game design is cohesiveness and disparate elements that might look ok on their own, but when it comes together it doesn’t work. So really be intentional about your design phase, ensure you have proper standards that your design is living up to, create mockups of what you want your screen space to look like before you start coding, and ultimately never stop being critical of what you’re looking at on the screen. When you think something is done, go over it once, twice, three more times. Keep asking yourself if it could be better. 

It’s painstaking work but it makes a huge difference in what the final output reads as.

replies.author: QcyqApps
replies.body: Thanks, that's actually very constructive feedback. I agree that UI polish and consistency are areas that need more attention. I think you're right that using AI doesn't remove the need for an eye for design and critical evaluation. Sometimes you need an outside perspective to notice things you've become blind to after working on a project for so long. I'll definitely take your suggestions

replies.author: alcarcalimo1950
replies.body:
Absolutely. And it’s still absolutely necessary to ask for feedback cause you’re right about blind spots.

It’s just helpful when you’re designing your game, to really refine the look you’re going for, including the little details. Really spec out everything, down to the pixel padding on a UI border, then when you give stuff to AI to do, it knows exactly what you’re looking for and isn’t just guessing. It keeps everything more cohesive and results in not having to go back and iterate as much. And if it still gets it wrong on the first pass, if you have a spec, you know exactly what to tell it to fix.
